div.head: A real-time system is characterized by its timely response with respect to e-aernal stimuli. A timely response usually consists of a series of tasks which must be scheduled and executed accordingly so that the controlled environment can function correctly. In this paper, we present the timing constraint Petri nets (or TCPNs for short) to facilitate the modeling and analysis of real-time systems. One of the analysis capabilities of TCPNs discussed in this paper is the schedulability analysis. Through a series of modeling, analysis, and iterative refinement, the sofmtare developer can verify whether an underlying specvcation will be schedulable with respect to the given timing requirements, all via the token game played in TCPN's. Nevertheless, the analysis presented here is to analyze the schedulability of real-time systems against the imposed timing constraints, rather than to elaborate a scheduling policy.
1: Introduction
div.p: A real-time system is characterized by its timely response with respect to external stimuli. Therefore, the correctness of a real-time system depends not only on the logical results of its behavior, but also on the time at which the results are produced [14]. In general, a proper response usually consists of a series of tasks execution, and a task in real-time systems is characterized by its start time, execution time, and deadline [15]. The process of computing and deciding a task sequence is called scheduling and the sequence is *This research was in part supported by National Science Foundation under grants CCR-8809381 and CCR-9106540. called a schedule. The process of verifying a schedule will meet the timing constraints is referred to as schedulability analysis [5,16,18]. It is well known that the specification and verification of real-time systems are much more difficult than non-real-time systems because the functionalities of real-time systems are time-related and whose correctness must take the imposed timing constraints into consideration [4]. Conventionally, timing constraint in a real-time system are defined as the temporal restriction between the occurrence of two events [3]. Dasarathy further classifies the timing constraints as different types, among which, we discuss three of them as follows: 1) the maximum timing constraint, which is the maximal amount of time that may elapse between the occurrence of two events; 2) the minimum timing constraint, which is the minimal amount of time that must elapse between the occurrence of two events; 3) the maximum durational timing constraint, which is the amount of time for that a task must last.

Petri nets (or PNs for short) [9] are gaining popularity in recent years because of their strong capability in modeling and analyzing concurrent systems. However, the concept of time is not explicitly provided in the original definition of Petri nets which limits their usability in real-time systems. In this paper, we present the timing constraint Petri nets which are the extended Petri nets designed to facilitate the modeling and analysis of real-time systems. In our approach, the modeling and analysis procedure is taken place from two perspectives: the functional property and the timing property. From the functional property point of view, the modeling and analysis is performed directly through the method of classic PNs to assert system's functional Correctness.

From the timing property point of view, the method of TCPNs are used to assert the correctness of timing behaviors. Since the functionality has been asserted using PNs before the timing property analysis begins, therefore, the functionality relationships among transitions are preserved in TCPNs along with the newly attached timing constraints.
Through the modeling and analysis using TCPN's, a series of iterating refinement is performed toward an asserted timing requirements specification.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the related work of extended Petri nets. Section 3 presents the definition of TCPNs. In Section 4, the schedulabiliy analysis using TCPNs is discussed along with an illustrated example. Finally, we conclude this paper by marking our future research in Section 5.

div.head: 2: Related Work
div.p: Many efforts are devoted to extending the classic Petri nets, and great progress can be found in the areas of temporal behavior analysis [ 1,2,4,7,8,10,17] and performance evaluation [6,11,12,13]. Timed Petri nets are first proposed by Ramchandani in [ 121 featuring the timing analysis of asynchronous concurrent systems. A timed Petri net is a net where each transition tj is associated with a delay time, del(($, indicating that the firing of 9 has to be delayed for del(tj) amount of time once it is enabled. Ramamoorthy and Ho [ll] further increase the use of timed Petri nets to the area of performance evaluation.

Time Petri nets are introduced by Merlin and Farber in [8] for analyzing the recoverability of communication protocols. A time Peui net (TPN) is a net where each transition tj is associated with a time interval, [min(tj), max(tj)], indicating that the tj is not allowed to fire before time TO+min(tj), may or may not fire between To+min(tj) and To+max(tj), and must fire after To+max(tj) once tj it is enabled at To. Leveson and Stolzy use time Petri nets to model a real-time system for safety analysis [7]. To perform the safety analysis, a reachability graph of the time Petri nets model regarding the system behavior is first constructed to determine whether a high-risk state will be reached. The timing constraints imposed to the modeled system can then be derived to avoid such high risk states. Berthomieu and Diaz propose an enumerative method to analyze the temporal behavior of a concurrent system [l]. Through the technique of reachability analysis used in time Petri nets, the authors claim that their method can exhaustively validate the behavior of the modeled system.

Peng and Shin use a generalized stochastic Petri net (GSPN) to model the real-time control activities in a distributed system [lo]. The modeled activities in GSPN are then formed as a sequence of homogeneous continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) for the probability analysis of missing deadline. Suzuki and Lu introduce a temporal Petri net by combining temporal logic and Peui nets together for the modeling and analysis of a concurrent system [17]. In temporal Petri nets, the timing constraints of a system are represented by the operations of temporal logic for analyzing the temporal relationships such as eventuality and faimess among system events.

Despite the efforts of the extended Petri nets in performance analysis, the existing versions of timerelated Petri nets are not suitable for specifying various timing constraints. Therefore, another time version of Petri nets, timing constraint Petri nets, are presented to overcome the above shortcomings and to use a systematic way to achieve modeling and analysis of real-time systems.

div.head: 3: Timing Constraint Petri Nets
div.p: TCPN's are the extension of Petri nets in conjunction with pairs of minimum timing constraints and maximum timing constraints attached on places, and durational timing constraints attached on transitions. The formal definition of TCPNs is presented here. A timing constraint Petri net is a tuple <P, T, F, C, D, M> where: P is a set of places, i.e., P=( p1, ..., pm}, Tis a set of transitions, i.e., T=(@,t1, ..., tn}, F is a set of arcs which connects places and transitions, C is a set of integer pairs, [TCmin(a,),TCmax(aj)],

where aj is either a place or a transition, D is a set of firing durations, TCdur(dj), where d, is a transition, and M is a set of marking with m-vector, {M(Pl) ,...,M(Pj),...,M(pm)}, where M(pj) denotes the numbers of token in place pj. MO denotes the initial marking.

TCPN's follow the same enabling rules of PN's and TPNs in which a transition tj is enabled if each input place of tj has at least one token. Nevertheless, the firing rules are different. In both PNs and TPNs, the firing of a transition is instantaneous which is assumed cost no time at all. However, in TCPNs, the firing of a transition takes a duration time. In PN's, a transition tj is firable once it is enabled, and tj is continually enabled and firable until either it is fired or is disabled by the firing of other transitions. In contrast, the firing of a transition tj is restricted in both TPNs and TCPNs so that it may only take place during a restricted period of time after tj is enabled. For example, let a transition tj with a time pair (min,max) be enabled at time To, the firing behavior of TPNs and TCPNs are as follows: In both nets, tj is enabled but cannot be fired before (To+min) and may or may not be fired during the time interval from (To+min) to (To+max). If tj has not been fired at (To+max), here comes the difference. In TPNs, tj must be fired after (To+max), while in TCPNs, tj can no longer be fired after (To+max).

div.head: 4: Schedulability Analysis Using TCPN's
div.p: In this section, we present the methods based on TCPNs to perform the schedulability analysis. We present the procedure of schedulability analysis through an illustrated example featuring a radar and missile controlling system called RAM. Through a series of modeling, analysis, and iterative refinement, the software developer can verify whether an underlying specification will be schedulable with respect to the given timing requirements, all via the token game played in TCPNs.

div.head: : Basic Concept
div.p: To perform the schedulability analysis, we start from the initial transition and verify each reachable transition from the initial transitions. If one transition is found not schedulable, there is no way that this specification can meet the timing requirements. Then, stop the analysis, either fix the design or change the timing requirements, then verify the schedulability of the modified transitions again till it is schedulable. The analysis and refinement will be repeated till an asserted specification is reached.

div.head: 4.2: Specification of RAM
div.p: In this subsection, we specify a radar and missile controlling system called RAM for the illustration of the analysis methods presented in the next subsection. In RAM, the radiation ray is spread, received and processed periodically. If no flying target is detected, no sporadic tasks will take place in the system. However, once a flying k?rget is detected, the detection of flying target serves as a stimulus to the system and a series of tasks then take place for responding to the stimulus timely. In RAM, a series of tasks consist of displaying the flying target on screen and requesting the computer and the commander to make a decision whether or not to launch a missile. If both the computer and the commander decide to launch a missile, then a launching command is issued and the missile is launched. Otherwise, the missile is not launched. In terms of functional requirements, the system must be able to launch a missile when the decision is made. In terms of timing requirements, the missile must be launched in time after the launching command has been made. The following requirements denoted by R# are used to specify the timing requirements of the RAM, and the time unit used here is second. R1: The radar detection of a flying target is performed every 15 seconds. (to) R2: After a flying target is detected, the information about the flying target (such as speed, location, height, etc.) must be prepared within 6 seconds.
The task of preparing information takes 3 seconds.

R3: After the information about the flying target is prepared, the system needs at least 2 seconds but no more than 4 seconds to display the flying target along with its related information on screen. The task of displaying the information takes 2 seconds.
R4: Once the flying target is displayed on screen, the commander needs at least 1 second, but no more than 4 seconds to make the launching decision. The task of human decision takes 5 seconds. ('3)

Therefore, we prolong the enabling time of p6 from 3 From the above definitions and illustration, we conclude the schedirlubility analysis using TCPN's as follows: If at least one of the transitions in a TCPN is not strongly schedulable with respect to the initial transition Q, then this net is not a schedulable net. In other words, the TCPN is not schedulable under the imposed timing constraints. Since TCPNs are the time extension of PN's, the following observation are made regarding some properties of PN's and TCPNs: Due to the stringent firing rules of TCPN's, the firing of a transition with TCdur can only be started and must be completed within the time pair (TCmin,TCmax), or the transition is disabled. Therefore, a live transition in PNs could become dead because of the imposed timing constraints. Similarly, a safe place in PNs is not necessary a safe place in TCPN's because in TCPN's, a non-schedulable transition will not be fired, and won't consume any token which will cause its input places accumulate tokens and makes the net non-safe. For a non-safe place pj in TCPNs, the output transitions of pj are most likely the cause of system performance bottleneck. The reason is that the input transitions of pj are generating more tokens than p.'s output transitions can consume.

The analysis presented so far is based totally on the specification in TCPNs before the real execution. For a safe and schedulable TCPN, we call that it is an asserted TCPN with respect to the given requirements specification. A similar analysis can be performed after the execution for the run-time testing and debugging, since the post-mortem analysis is based on the collected execution histories [19,20], if any unsafe place or unschedulable transition is detected, then the detected J places and the transitions are the most likely location causing the timing constraint violations.

div.head: 5: Conclusion and Future Research
div.p: TCPN's are presented in this paper for the schedulability analysis of a real-time system. Our schedulability analysis always computes the worst case of the scheduling of a requirements specification with respect to the imposed timing constraints. Once all transitions in a TCPN are verified to be strongly schedulable with respect to the initial transition, we said such specification is asserted with respect to its timing requirements. In addition, throughout the example of modeling and analyzing a radar and missile controlling system, we successfully demonstrate that it is possible to perform the specification and the scheduling analysis using the Same representation.

The analysis presented in this paper is based on the requirements specification in a TCPN before its execution. However, we believe the similar analysis can be applied as well to the run-time testing and debugging. In our future research, we will integrate our former research results [19,20,21,22] with the schedulability analysis method presented in this paper. The target code of an asserted specification will be executed on a realistic or simulated target system to collect its run-time information. Once the run-time information is collected, along with our visualization and debugging method, the schedulability analysis is able to detect the run-time errors with respect to the timing requirements from specification phase.
